question: What is the nurse's main job when assessing a patient's diet?

options.C: Collecting and evaluating food intake data

explanation: You've got this! Nurses gather information on what patients eat to spot any nutrition risks early and plan the best care possible. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T006#GNS227_U5_T006_h1)

question: Why should a nurse ask about a patient's cultural background during a dietary assessment?

options.A: Food choices are deeply tied to beliefs and traditions
options.B: Cultural habits prevent patients from ever developing deficiencies
options.C: Dietary guidelines are identical for every human population
options.D: Hospital kitchens only prepare culturally neutral foods

explanation: Great thinking! Knowing a patient's food culture helps you suggest meals that they will actually enjoy and stick to. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T006#GNS227_U5_T006_h1)

question: Why is it so helpful to check a patient's diet early on?

options.A: Predicting future genetic mutations in children
options.B: Determining the exact date of hospital discharge
options.C: Detecting nutrient deficiencies before physical signs appear
options.D: Calculating the financial cost of grocery shopping

explanation: Spotting nutrition problems early means you can jump in and help before things get worse. Excellent nursing intuition! [learn more](GNS227_U5_T006#GNS227_U5_T006_h2)

question: How does keeping track of a patient's starting diet help the healthcare team?

options.A: It measures if nutrition interventions are working over time
options.B: It proves the patient is following hospital rules strictly
options.C: It eliminates the need to ever weigh the patient again
options.D: It replaces the need for laboratory blood investigations

explanation: Spot on! Having a clear starting point lets you track progress and see if your nutrition plan is actually helping the patient get better. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T006#GNS227_U5_T006_h2)

question: What does a 24-hour dietary recall ask the patient to do?

options.A: Weigh every meal on a digital scale for a full week
options.B: List all food and drink consumed over the past day
options.C: Write down future grocery shopping lists in advance
options.D: Fast completely for 24 hours before a blood test

explanation: Easy peasy! A 24-hour recall simply asks the patient to remember and list everything they ate and drank during the last 24 hours. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T006#GNS227_U5_T006_h3)

question: What is the main benefit of using a Food Frequency Questionnaire?

options.A: It captures long-term dietary patterns and habits
options.B: It prevents patients from ever forgetting yesterday's lunch
options.C: It requires zero participation from the patient
options.D: It provides exact gram weights for every single meal

explanation: You got it! FFQs give you a broad look at a patient's eating habits over weeks or months, rather than just focusing on yesterday's meals. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T006#GNS227_U5_T006_h3)

question: Which method gives the most precise and exact picture of what a patient eats?
explanation: Spot on! Weighing the food before eating and measuring any leftovers gives you the most accurate data possible. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T006#GNS227_U5_T006_h4)

question: A patient keeps a 5-day food diary on the ward, but the nurse notices the meals look unusually tiny. What is the most likely reason?

options.A: Weighed food records are completely useless in hospital settings
options.B: The patient is secretly eating large amounts of hidden snacks
options.C: The patient may be altering intake or underreporting to simplify logging
options.D: The patient's metabolic rate has suddenly dropped to zero

explanation: Exactly. Writing down every little thing can be tiring, so patients sometimes eat less or forget to log certain items! [learn more](GNS227_U5_T006#GNS227_U5_T006_h4)

question: Which nutrient intake value is set high enough to cover almost all healthy people?
explanation: You're doing great! The RDA is set high up to make sure it meets the nutritional needs of about 97 to 98 percent of healthy folks. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T006#GNS227_U5_T006_h5)

question: Why is it important for nurses to know the Tolerable Upper Intake Level (UL)?

options.A: It tells the nurse the minimum daily protein a patient needs
options.B: It measures the total fiber content in local staple foods
options.C: It helps identify the threshold where nutrient supplements become toxic
options.D: It calculates the exact basal metabolic rate of a toddler

explanation: Smart thinking! The UL warns us when vitamins or minerals cross the line from healthy to harmful. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T006#GNS227_U5_T006_h5)

question: What does 'social desirability bias' mean when assessing a patient's diet?

options.A: Reporting healthier eating habits to please the healthcare provider
options.B: Refusing to eat hospital meals due to cultural beliefs
options.C: Forgetting to log snacks and sugary beverages during the day
options.D: Failing to understand how to use a standard food scale

explanation: Patients want to impress us! They sometimes claim they eat better than they actually do just to please their nurse. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T006#GNS227_U5_T006_h6)

question: Which food items do patients most often forget to mention during a diet recall?

options.A: Main staple foods like rice and yams

explanation: It's easy to forget small bites and sips! Extra snacks, drinks, and cooking oils are the most commonly missed items. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T006#GNS227_U5_T006_h6)

question: What is a fitting nursing diagnosis when a dietary assessment shows poor eating habits?

options.A: Risk for Excessive Intravenous Infusion Rate
options.C: Imbalanced Nutrition: Less Than Body Requirements
options.D: Impaired Ability to Perform Major Surgery

explanation: Spot on! This standard nursing diagnosis matches findings when a patient isn't getting enough nutrients from their food. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T006#GNS227_U5_T006_h7)

question: An older patient only eats tea and bread every day. What is the best next step for the nurse?

options.A: Collaborate with a dietitian to plan nutrient-dense meals and snacks
options.B: Scold the patient for having poor eating habits
options.C: Document that the patient has perfect nutritional status
options.D: Discharge the patient immediately since they are eating something

explanation: You're a natural! Once you spot a nutritional gap, teaming up with a dietitian is the best way to help the patient eat healthier. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T006#GNS227_U5_T006_h7)
